CONDOR ST URBAN WILD, EAST BOSTON: WASTE MANAGEMENT WILL SPEND APPROXIMATELY $1,200,000 TO HELP THE CITY OF BOSTON'S PARKS AND RECREATION DEPT BUILD AN URBAN WILD ON 4.5 ACRES OF FILL BORDERING CHELSEA CREEK. WHEN COMPLETE, THE PROJECT WILL RECREATE SALT MARSH AND UPLAND HABITATS, AND CREATE A PATH AND BOARDWALK ACCESS SYSTEM. AT PRESENT THIS IS A FENCED, TRASH STREWN, CONTAMINATED SITE OWNED BY THE CITY AND SUBJECT TO CLEANUP UNDER CHAPTER 21E. ALTHOUGH THE PARKS DEPT MUST REMOVE SOME OF THE CONTAMINATED SOIL IN ORDER TO COMPLY WITH CHAPTER 21E, IT LACKS THE FUNDS TO RESTORE THIS AS AN  URBAN WILD  AND TO PROVIDE QUALITY OPEN SPACE FOR THE COMMUNITY. TREES AND PLANTS WILL PROVIDE AIR QUALITY BENEFITS, WILDLIFE HABITAT WILL BE RESTORED, AND WATER QUALITY WILL BE ENHANCED THROUGH THE CREATION OF SALT MARSH.  TO ENSURE THE CONTINUING VITALITY OF THE PROJECT, WASTE MANAGEMENT WILL PAY $10,000 A YEAR OVER FIFTEEN YEARS TO HELP THE CITY WITH THE MAINTENANCE OF THE SITE (MOWING, REPAIR OF SALT MARSH DAMAGE, ETC.) AND WILL PROVIDE $12,500 A YEAR FOR FIFTEEN YEARS TO A LOCAL COMMUNITY STEWARDSHIP, AND IMPLEMENT AN EDUCATION COMPONENT WITH LOCAL SCHOOLS.

DIESEL SCHOOL BUS PROJECT:  WASTE MANAGEMENT WILL SPEND $1,440,000 TO FUND THE INSTALLATION OF PARTICULATE FILTERS ON APPROXIMATELY 16O SCHOOL BUSES, AND PAY FOR THE INCREMENTAL COST OF ULTRA-LOW SULFUR DIESEL FUEL FOR USE OF THESE BUSES UNTIL JULY 2006. ESTIMATED COSTS ARE $5000 PER BUS FOR THE FILTERS, AND 20 TO 30 CENTS PER GALON FOR THE INCREMENTAL COSTS OF FUEL AND DELIVERY. THIS WILL LOWER THE PARTICULATE EMISSIONS FROM THESE DIESEL SCHOOL BUSES BY APPROXIMATELY 95%, DRAMATICALLY REDUCING THE CHILDREN'S EXPOSURE TO ASTHMA TRIGGERS AN CARCINOGENS. (EPA REGULATIONS WILL REQUIRE EXTRA-LOW SULFUR FUEL IN 2006, BUT WILL NOT REQUIRE THE INSTALLATION OF PARTICULATE FILTERS ON EXISTING BUSES.) THE PROJECT BUSES WILL BE OPERATED FROM THE READVILLE DEPOT, WHICH SERVES A NUMBER OF THE BOSTON COMMUNITIES WITH THE HIGHEST ASTHMA RATES. INCLUDING ROXBURY, DORCHESTER, MATTAPAN AND HYDE PARK.

MBTA WILL CONDUCT TWO SEPs. THE FIRST IS TO SWITCH MBTA's 33 SOUTH STATION TRAINS TO LOW-SULFUR DIESEL FUEL FOR THREE YEARS, AT A COST OF APPROXIMATELY $1 MILLION. MBTA USES SEVEN MILLION GALLONS OF DIESEL FUEL PER YEAR IN ITS SOUTH STATION TRAINS. THE SEP WILL REDUCE APPROXIMATELY 32 TONS OF PARTICULATE MATTER AND 429 TONS OF SULFUR DIOXIDE FROM THE AIR AROUND BOSTON OVER THREE YEARS. I.E., APPROXIMATELY 11 TONS OF PRATICULATES, AND 143 TONS OF SULFUR DIOXIDE. THE SOUTH STATION TRAINS RUN THROUGH BOSTON'S POOREST, MOST ASTHMA PRONE AREAS. THE SEP WILL END IN JUNE 2007, WHEN EPA's PROPOSED  OFF-ROAD  RULE WILL REQUIRE USE OF LOW SULFUR DIESEL FUEL IN LOCOMOTIVES. FOR ITS SECOND SEP, MBTA WILL DONATE LAND SO THAT AN EXISTING MYSTIC RIVER BIKE PATH MAY EVENTUALLY BE EXTENDED TO BOSTON, PROMOTING BICYCLE COMMUTING. THE MYSTIC RIVER RUNS THROUGH SOME OF TH MOST DENSE, DIVERSE, AND ENVIRONMENTALLY IMPACTED COMMUNITIES IN MASSACHUSETTS.
ALTERNATIVE SEP:  IF ONE OF THE SEPs DOES NOT WORK OUT, MBTA MAY BRING LOCOMOTIVES INTO EARLY COMPLIANCE WITH EPA's  TIER 0  LOCOMOTIVE EMISSION STANDARDS.

Warren Avenue Mitigation SEP
The Respondent shall undertake all necessary actions to design and build a Warren Avenue sewerage collection system from the Narragansett Bay Commission (NBC) interceptor tie-in outwards to Woonasquatucket Avenue with the intent of eliminating basement backups in the area.  The Respondent shall comply with all state and local laws and regulations, as well as NBC requirements, including all necessary permits or approvals, in undertaking such actions.  This work shall include the following steps:
1.Solicit Bids for Sewerage System Engineering Study and Design 
By July 15, 2010, the Respondent shall develop and publish a Request for Proposal to retain a professional engineering consultant, licensed in Rhode Island, with significant experience and expertise in the study and design of wastewater collections systems, to complete an engineering evaluation of, and design for, a wastewater collection system on Warren Avenue.  The evaluation and design shall require, at a minimum, an assessment, as necessary, of how current conditions cause or contribute to backups of sewage into residential properties on Warren Avenue, and the development of plans and specifications, including any changes to plumbing systems in the affected residential properties.  All necessary coordination with relevant State agencies and the NBC shall be the Respondents responsibility.  The survey and plan shall employ accepted engineering standards for sewer conveyance, such as TR-16, RIDEM Sanitary Sewer Design Policies, and any other relevant design protocols, in a manner that will protect public health, private and public properties, and the environment.
2.Awarding of Engineering Contract      
By August 15, 2010, the Respondent shall award a contract for the engineering and design of a wastewater collection system on Warren Avenue in accordance with the Request for Proposal described in paragraph 1 above. 
3.Approval and permitting of Engineering Plan
By September 30, 2010, the Respondent shall have a final engineering plan and required permits and approvals.
4.Solicit Bids for Sewerage System Construction 
By September 30, 2010, the Respondent shall develop and publish a Request for Proposals for the construction of the wastewater collection system for Warren Avenue in accordance with the approved engineering plan.   
5.Awarding of Construction Contract
By October 29, 2010, the Respondent shall award a contract for the construction of a wastewater collection system on Warren Avenue in accordance with the approved engineering plan.   
6.Commencement of Construction
By November 12, 2010, the Respondent shall commence construction of the wastewater collection system on Warren Avenue in accordance with the approved engineering plan.   Construction will be monitored by Town officials to ensure construction is in accordance with the approved plans and specifications.  Adequate and timely notification will be made to private sewer users regarding any interruption in sewer service, as well as any other inconveniences related to construction.  
7.Substantial Completion of construction
By December 10, 2010, the Respondent shall have substantially completed construction of the wastewater collection system on Warren Avenue in accordance with the approved engineering plan.

City of Meriden, Connecticut, Department of Public Utilities, Water
Division, proposes this Scope of Work for the Supplemental Environmental Project ( SEP ) that
would be performed in conjunction with the Consent Agreement and Final Order resulting from
the above-referenced complaint ( Complaint ). Dennis Waz, Director of Public Utilities for the
City, provided the information contained in this proposal.
The Meriden Department of Public Utilities ( Meriden Public Utilities ) already has
reduced the threat posed by chlorine gas used in its water treatment system by converting its
main water treatment facility. Broad Brook Water Treatment Plant, from chlorine gas to sodium
hypochlorite following the inspection that gave rise to the Complaint. This conversion will be
finalized in September 2015, at a cost of more than $17.9 million.
However, Meriden Public Utilities has seven additional locations utilizing gaseous
chlorine (in 150 lb. cylinders) as part of its system. Having investigated various disinfection
alternatives to the use of gaseous chlorine gas, Meriden Public Utilities proposes to eliminate the
use of chlorine at these other water treatment facilities and subsurface drinking water wells. Of
the seven locations, three are water filtration plants and the remaining four locations are drinking
water wells; a table identifying these facilities appears below.
Meriden Public Utilities is proposing to replace the existing gaseous chlorine gas systems
at these seven facilities with calcium hypochlorite tablet feeders. Prior to converting each of
these chlorine systems, Meriden Public Utilities has to secure approval from the State of
Connecticut's Department of Health, Drinking Water Section for the conversion. Conversion to
calcium hypochlorite tablet feeders involves purchase of seven tablet feeder units with load cells
to measure the quantity of calcium hypochlorite tablets for usage and reporting purposes. In addition to those units, redundant pumps (both chemical mixing and chemical feed) and piping modifications would be required. Each unit would also have to be integrated into the existing SCADA system.  Each facility would be required to have spare parts, pumps, and other equipment should a system failure occur. Once each calcium hypochlorite system is installed and commissioned, and reliability has been demonstrated, the existing gaseous chlorine system at the facility would be decommissioned.

a.	Lynn Public Schools SEP:  This SEP was developed by Garelick Farms in consultation with the Lynn Public Schools. It has three elements. The first is to have Clean Harbors remove unneeded science laboratory chemicals from Lynn Classical High School, a public school, and properly dispose of them. The chemicals include flammable and toxic materials. The estimated cost of this component of the project is approximately $4,500. The second component is to provide science laboratory safety equipment at three public middle schools in Lynn. The equipment includes first aid kits, and safety goggles, gloves and aprons to help protect the students when they handle hazardous chemicals. The equipment cost is estimated to be approximately $16,500. The third component is for a Garelick Farms Environmental Health and Safety professional to provide HAZCOM 2012-compliant training to the Lynn Public Schools Assistant Director of Curriculum and Instruction/Science K-12 and four teachers from each of the following schools:  Classical High School, and the Thurgood Marshall, Breed, and Pickering Middle Schools. This training will assist the schools in the safe and proper handling and disposal of hazardous chemicals.

Emergency Response Equipment SEP:  The second SEP is for Garelick Farms to provide updated equipment and training to the Lynn Fire Department to improve its ability to respond to hazardous materials incidents.  The training includes basic and extended technical training classes as well as ammonia tactical response classes, which will provide the fire department with the most updated techniques when responding to emergencies that involve anhydrous ammonia or similar chemicals. The equipment that will be provided includes handheld ammonia sensors (as well as pumps, charging units, and a maintenance/calibration contract for such sensors), and specialized personal protective equipment, such as Kevlar coats and pants, gloves, and boots.  There are several RMP facilities within a few miles of this plant, so the training and equipment will support the City�s ability to respond to hazardous materials incidents at other facilities, as well. The total cost of the equipment upgrades and training is $195,000.

Safety Upgrades at the Garelick Farms Lynn Facility:  The third SEP is to expand the ammonia detection system at the Lynn, MA Facility beyond industry standards to include sensors in pressure release valve headers in multiple locations at the Facility.  These will allow for early detection of outdoor releases and, together with automatic valves and controls, provide a means to shut down the source of the overpressure to minimize the ammonia release.  The SEP also includes the installation of a Win911 notification system, which interfaces with the Facility�s ammonia refrigeration programmable logic controller to automatically send alerts by email, text, or phone call about any alarm conditions from a central system.  These alerts can be sent to the appropriate plant personnel and emergency responders, thus reducing the time to alert personnel to an ammonia release or to conditions that might cause a release.  The total cost of this SEP is approximately $100,000.

Defendants jointly and severally shall establish an escrow account in the amount of one million dollars ($1,000,000) to fund the SEP.  Pursuant to the SEP, PRASA shall evaluate Non-PRASA Systems consisting of privately-owned and operated water supplies in Puerto Rico, that are considered by EPA, in consultation with the Puerto Rico Department of Health ( PRDOH ), as substandard and which fail to comply with applicable safe drinking water standards.  The Evaluations will serve to determine what actions can be taken to bring the Non-PRASA Systems into compliance with such safe drinking water standards.  The primary objectives of the Non-PRASA System Sep are to:
-Connect Non-PRASA Systems to PRASA, to the extent practicalbe.
-Install disinfection in selected Non-PRASA Systems.
-Reduce the overall number of Non-PRASA Systems that derive drinking water from untreated surface water sources.
-Reduce the number of positive bacteriological results in Non-PRASA Systems.
-Provide training to qualified individuals administering the Non-PRASA Systems to ensure proper operation and maintencnce of system improvements.

The innovative use of microwave ovens to minimize the generation of hazardous waste and energy in college and high school hands on laboratory chemistry experiments. 

Overview
Microwave-enhanced chemistry is the science of applying microwave irradiation to chemical reactions. Microwave-assisted reactions can be green chemistry methods, as they are often run neat or in aqueous solutions minimizing the need for organic solvents.

This Supplemental Environmental Project (SEP) accomplishes Pollution Prevention by eliminating or reducing the need for solvents and reducing energy needs required in experiments though the use of microwave-enhanced chemistry. In addition, Environmental Outreach will be employed to potentially expand the scope of the Pollution Prevention benefits to high school chemistry programs throughout New Jersey (and possibly beyond). A minimum of $125,000 will be spent on this SEP.

Elements
  Evaluate previous work done regarding green chemistry experiments by doing a full literature review of previous work done in high schools and universities as applied to instructional laboratories.
  Determine how the college and high school curriculum might be enhanced (by raising the awareness of sustainability and pollution prevention) with the use of microwave technology.
  Evaluate green chemistry guides developed to date for use in NJIT laboratories. 
  Purchase one (1) CEM Corporation Microwave and associated blowout valves for use at NJIT and three (3) smaller microwaves for use by participating high schools. 
  Develop no fewer than three (3) experiments at NJIT that would be suitable for use as part of a chemistry curriculum and measure the amount of solvent and energy reduction achieved with the use of microwave-enhanced practices rather than traditional chemistry practices.
  Conduct two half-day focus group exercises with chemistry educators from no less than three (3) local high schools. 
  Incorporate applicable experiments into laboratory instructional materials for NJIT freshmen through junior level chemistry courses. These experiments will be implemented at NJIT and will be designed and publicized to encourage adoption elsewhere in the country. The pollution prevention resulting from these experiments during this time will be tracked by computing the savings in chemical usage and energy at NJIT. 
  Develop new components of a Unified Instructional Guide for Laboratory Chemistry Experiments On Green Chemistry, a manual discussing the methodology for conducting Green Chemistry laboratory experiments in both high school and college level classes and the environmental benefits of performing such experiments. Make both hard copies and electronic copies for distribution (through posting on the NJIT website), at no charge to recipients.
  Prepare a(n) account/article/publication/report of the benefits of the use of microwave-enhanced chemistry experiments in high school and college level chemistry laboratories for publication and place this article on the NJIT website. 
  Prepare a Fact Sheet summarizing NJITs account/article/publication/report and containing the link to the NJITs website article; and distribute this to colleges and nearby high schools. 
  Submit quarterly progress reports, a written milestone report, and a SEP Completion Report to EPA.

Installation of Wastewater Evaporation System - John Hassall, Inc. will commit to spending at least $33,000 on installing a gas-fired water evaporator system to reduce discharge of its wastewater into the Cedar Creek POTW in Nassau County, New York.  Nassau County periodically collects and analyses water samples to monitor compliance with its discharge parameters.  The ideal goal of this proposed SEP Project would be to ultimately achieve zero discharge into the sewer system by evaporating off the water.  This system will also result in a reduction in the solid residue due to the reduction of chemical treatment of the water.  The waste stream is currently treated with carbon dioxide to adjust the Ph, hydrated lime to precipitate metals, and calcium chloride and carbon to remove emulsified oils and then filtered through a diatomaceous earth filter before being discharged to the POTW.  The solid residue contains chromium, copper, nickel and hexane.  As part of this system a biological pretreatment is being considered to also be added to reduce or eliminate the concentration of oils and grease and suspended solids prior to evaporation to prevent plate out of contaminants on the evaporator heating core.  The evaporation system is more costly than chemical treatment and sending the solid residue to a landfill.  Each truckload of metal contaminated residue would be reduced to about four 55 gallon drums.  It is estimated to cost about 4 cents more per gallon of water treated with the evaporator system than by chemical treatment.  Initially, the company would commit to reducing its water discharge by about 105,000 gallons per year for at least 5 years.  The company currently discharges from 250,000 up to 500,000 gallons of wastewater per year to the POTW.  The ultimate ideal goal would be to totally switch over to the evaporator system, but the switchover is dependent on the economy and production levels.

ACuPowder commits to executing a Pollution Reduction SEP to better reduce the metal dust particulates that are generated during the manufacture of metal powders in several of their production buildings.  ACuPowder intends to install a Central Particulate Dust Vacuum Collection System supplemented by two mobile particulate dust collectors.  ACuPowder manufactures metal powders and alloys that are used in the manufacture of mechanical components, including gears and self-lubricating bearings.  The powders include primarily copper, tin, zinc and nickel.  The companys current emission capture rates are within the limits allowed by the companys air permit issued by the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection, but near the upper PEL limits of those metals set by OSHA.  The facilty generates approximately 1,000lbs of particulate fugitive dust per year.  With the addition of the SEP technologies and the existing dust collection equipment,it is estimated that only 0.3lbs of dust would potentially be released to the environment.   The high efficiency HEPA filters to be installed in the dust vacuum collection system as part of this SEP have a removal efficiency of 99.9%.   Improving the rates of removal would benefit both the workers health at work and home and the surrounding community by substantially minimizing the amount of dust that is inhaled or escapes the building through traffic in and out of the building by production workers and fork lift trucks entering and leaving the building.  The metal dust that accumulates on the floor, walls, equipment, ceilings and piping from each manufacturing process line is currently manually swept and collected in a container to be recycled.

Vessel Pressure Wash System and Wash Water Recycle Tank: 
This SEP exemplifies Pollution Prevention by protecting natural resources through the conservation of water through the  collection of the process tank flush water for reuse resulting in reduced water consumption.  The company currently uses up to 100 gallons of water per wash which is discharged to the sanitary sewer.  With the addition of the wash system spray head, water usage would be reduced by approximately 50% and solids could more efficiently settle before the wastewater was discharged into the sewer.  This would also allow more water to be recycled back into the process line, thus reducing the total effluent to the sewer by 25%.

The reduction in water usage clearly exemplifies Pollution Prevention through the conservation of water and Pollution Reduction through the reduction of suspended solid contaminants in the sewer effluent.

Revere has enclosed smelting and refining operations and operates the enclosure with negative pressure to contain fugitive emissions. For this reason, Revere will enclose three sides of the bottom section of the slag reverberatory baghouse (SRF) with an enclosure of metal decking material sealed at the top and bottom with foam closer strips and caulking. The panels will be 13 feet high by 66 linear feet. This second layer of containment will reduce the risk of any future releases of lead to the community by adding another layer of prevention during maintenance activities or in the event of unpredicted releases of baghouse dust. The walls will act as a windbreak and partial containment of the hoppers, slide gates and conveyers so that any lead dust that may escape the equipment does not readily become airborne, and thus cleaning would be able to be initiated prior to any environmental release. The facility states that it currently meets industry standards and that this addition would be above and beyond any current EPA requirements and would meet all building codes. The total one-time expenditure for the purchase and installation of these walls will be $55,000. THE SEP CONSISTS OF TWO COMPONENTS, THE FIRST BEING THE INSTALLATION OF ADDITIONAL CONDENSERS AT THE PLANT AND THE SECOND BEING THE INSTALLATION OF AMMONIA SENSORS.   THE FACILITY USES AMMONIA AS A COOLANT.  THE SIZE OF THE CONDENSERS USED IN OF THE CURRENT AMMONIA SYSTEM REQUIRES THAT THE AMMONIA BE CIRCULATED THROUGHOUT THE FACILITY AT  HIGH  HEAD PRESSURE .  UNFORTUNATELY, THE HIGH HEAD PRESSURE CREATES A HIGH POTENTITAL FOR THE RELEASE OF AMMONIA FROM THE SYSTEM WHEN THE HEAD PRESSURE RISES, DUE IN PART TO HIGH OUTSIDE TEMPERATURES DURING WARM WEATHER, AND EXCEEDS THE PRESSURE AT WHICH THE SYSTEM'S ESCAPTE VALVES OPEN.  THE SEP PROVIDES FOR THE INSTALLATION OF ADDITIONAL CONDENSERS, WHICH WILL LOWER THE HEAD PRESSURE NEEDED TO OPERATE THE SYSTEM EFFECTIVELY, AND IN TURN GREATLY REDUCE THE LIKELIHOOD OF FUTURE RELEASES OF AMMONIA INTO THE ENVIRONMENT.

IN THE RELEASE THAT OCCURRED ON JULY 17, 2001, APPROXIMATELY 191 POUNDS OF AMMONIA WERE RELEASED INTO THE ENVIRONMENT.   IT IS DIFFICULT, HOWEVER, TO PREDICT THE SIZE OF THE RELEASES THAT WILL BE AVOIDED BY THE SEP.

Solids extracted from the process wastewater will be reused as fuel for process heaters, reducing the raw wood fuel consumption for that purpose by approximately 5%. General Iron is required to carry out the following projects.  First, they are required to perform a project to retrofit municipal diesel vehicles within the City of Chicago by installing pollution control devices to reduce the emissions of particulate matter and hydrocarbons.  The value of this SEP will be $315,000 and is to be completed within one year of the effective date of the Consent Decree.  Second, General Iron is required to participate in a series of gas-powered lawnmower buy-back events.  The value of this SEP will be $90,000 and is to be completed within five years of the effective date of the Consent Decree.  Third, General Iron is required to install an extensive Green Roof System on a building at its facility.  The value of this SEP will be at least $35,000 and is to be completed within one year of the effective date of the Consent Decree.  Fourth, General Iron is required to cleanup, restore, rebuild, re-vegetate, and maintain the river edge of its property along the North Branch of the Chicago River.  The value of this SEP will be $310,000 and General Iron is required to plant the natural vegetation within 2 years of the effective date of the Consent Decree and maintain the project for a period of five years from the effective date of the Consent Decree.

M & M Drying must spend by December 31, 2006 at least $330,000 to complete a SEP designed to protect the environment and public health.  The SEP consists of buying and remediating a 3.09 acre parcel of property next to its current facility in Minerva, Ohio, known as the Structural Stoneware property. The building and the permanent cap must cover approximately 75% of the property and any other areas of the property not covered by the sound barrier mound.  This property was formerly used and allegedly contaminated by another company.  The property contains a waste pile with both fired and unfired clay tile and miscellaneous debris from a tile making facility.  There may be lead and cadmium in the debris left on the property.  The state of Ohio has requested that there should be information in the corrective measures work plan for this property on managing hazardous waste, controlling storm water, and controlling fugitive dust during construction.  There should also be information on fencing the area between the site and the neighboring apartment complex, on operation and maintenance of the engineered controls and on an environmental covenant for the property.

Ralston will reduce pollution by reducing the energy needed to cool its two powerhouse air compressors.  Ralston needs 207 tons of cooling to remove the 2,484,000 BTU/hr of heat rejection produced by the two compressors, which it currently gets through a Trane chiller, which requires 141 KW to generate 207 tons of cooling.  To save energy, Ralston will stop using the Trane chiller and install a cooling system that circulates an 87°F propylene glycol solution through the compressors to absorb the heat they give off.  A Marley one-cell unit will provide the necessary cooling.  It provides 308 tons of cooling based on the manufacturer specification sheet.  Unlike the Trane chiller, the Marley unit itself requires no energy to operate; the total amount of power needed to cool the system comes from the auxiliary equipment, which consists of two 7.5 hp fans, a 15 hp circulation pump, and a 5 hp spray pump.  This auxiliary equipment requires 23 KW to run, which is 193 KW less than with using the Trane chiller.  Ralston states that this reduction in power will save 1,544,000 kwh of energy each year, based on operating approximately 8,000 hours a year.  According to a July 2000 report from the Department of Energy, the estimated CO2 emissions rate from the generation of electric power is 1.68 lbs CO2 per kwh in Ralstons location.  This equates to 1,297 tons of CO2 emissions reduced per year.

Proposed SEP: Implementation of an Environmental Management System
The EMS will be a system of maintaining environmental compliance with applicable regulations. The system, however, goes beyond just compliance. The EMS will also provide a system of checks and balances for the IDOC facilities. Once the IDOC is involved with the EMS, a site manager makes routine site visits to the facilities. During these site visits, all aspects of the facilities environmental programs are reviewed, records are checked and updated, training is conducted and documented, deficiencies are recorded, reporting to appropriate agencies is completed if required, and a closeout meeting is conducted with upper management where any issues noted during the inspection are reviewed. Any issues requiring further attention are disseminated to the appropriate personnel where they are addressed.
Quarterly site inspections will be conducted at the following IDOC facilities:
1. Indiana State Prison
2. Westville Correctional
3. Miami Correctional
4. Pendleton Correctional
5. Plainfield Correctional
6. Putnamville Correctional
7. Wabash Valley Correctional

The EMS will check on the status of the actions conducted in the subsequent routine site inspections. Following the completion of each site visit, a formal report is submitted to the facility with written documentation as to the issues discussed in the closeout
meeting. Action items and responsible parties are spelled out clearly as part of the report, as are consequences of non-compliance. All documentation for the EMS is placed on a site specific, password protected website

Radiac is required to implement a pollution prevention SEP to eliminate at least 10 percent of the naphthalene utilized in their process. The project will cost $95,000 and up to 20 months to implement.  Specifically, the project will require the company to utilize an alternative pore formers in place of naphthalene which will allow for a viable, salable product.  Any alternate pore formers cannot be listed as a Hazardous Air Pollutant in Section 112 of the Clean Air Act.  The company must comply with a naphthalene usage limit per unit of product which results in a 10 percent reduction from prior levels.  Since the facility will be utilizing 10 percent less naphthalene in their process, or 6,000 pounds per year less (when utilizing 60,000 pounds per year).  Total emissions after the SEP is implemented is 1,620 pounds per year.  Compared to the emissions prior to the SEP implementation at 1,800 pounds per year, the SEP will reduce 180 pounds of napthalene per year, in addition to small reductions of natural gas combustion emissions at the thermal oxidizers of nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide.

ACC has been using an air compressor and supply piping that is outdated and not energy efficient. The Company proposes to replace this old technology with new, energy-efficient parts by installing an energy-efficient air compressor. The energy efficient air compressor is a variable speed compressor that will work on an �on demand� basis to reduce consumption needed to produce the required air for the facility. Energy use is estimated to be significantly reduced due to the improved �on demand� technology. Current annual compressor electrical usage is approximately 2,496 kW, and would be reduced to approximately 1,622 kW. Industrial compressors utilize oil for lubrication, creating an oil and water condensate, which contains hydrocarbons and other contaminants that make it a hazardous waste. Installation of an oil water separator will be used to collect and filter oil from the condensate created by the compressor and dryer systems, thus reducing the amount of hazardous waste generated. The new system will also have a cycling dryer system which will further reduce energy consumption by trimming down to meet system demand instead of running constantly.

Environmental Benefits:
This project will result in reduced energy consumption by the facility and will contribute to the
overall reduction of pollutants associated with electric power generation. The energy efficient air
compressor is expected to reduce energy consumption up to 35%. It will reduce fuel and electricity usage for heating and cooling and day-to-day operations. These reductions will reduce air emissions of particulate matter, volatile organic carbon compounds, nitrogen oxides, and other pollutants associated with the combustion of fuel and generation of electricity. It will also
contribute to a reduction in peak loads on the electric power grid. The project will help prevent
pollution by reducing the electricity needed for compressed air systems, thereby reducing air
emissions and improving air quality. The project will also result in a reduction in waste condensate that is sent offsite for disposal.

Nexus:
This proposed pollution prevention project has a sufficient nexus to the underlying alleged
violations. It prevents pollution at its source, before it is generated, by reducing the quantity and
toxicity of pollutants, including air pollutants and hazardous waste from condensate. The
reduction in fuel and electricity usage will reduce air emissions of particulate matter, volatile
organic carbon compounds, nitrogen oxides, and other pollutants associated with the combustion
of fuel and generation of electricity. When atmospheric air is compressed, there is surplus water
that condenses to a liquid. This water mixes with other airborne constituents along with
lubricant/coolant from the industrial compressor, creating hazardous waste. The hazardous waste
generated from the outdated industrial compressor is then handled according to EPA disposal
requirements. The SEP proposes the installation of an oil water separator to collect and filter the
oil from the condensate, thereby reducing the amount of hazardous waste generated. The project
directly addresses pollutants and effects caused by pollutants. It will be implemented on site,
where the activity of concern relating to hazardous waste took place.

THE SEP WILL REDUCE AIR EMISSIONS AND REDUCE THE AMOUNT OF  HAZARDOUS WASTE BURNED IN THE STEAM GENERATORS BY RECOVERINGPROPYLENE, WHICH CAN BE USED IN ANOTHER PROCESS AND SOLD.   THE RESPONDENT PROPOSES TO USE A DESTRUCTION EFFICIENCY OF  99.9% SO A STANDARD EXEMPTION CAN BE USED AND NO PERMIT A-  MENDMENT WILL BE NECESSARY. THIS WILL RESULT IN AN AIR EMIS-SION REDUCTION OF APPROXIMATELY 2,190 LBS/YR OF VOLATILE OR-GANIC COMPOUNDS (VOC'S). ONCE THE VOC'S ARE REMOVED, A CAR- BON STREAM CAN THEN BE RECOVERED AS PROPANE. Zoo Storm Water Wetland SEP - Runoff entering the storm sewer system from the Dallas Zoo comes primarily from rainwater and from wash water used to clean animal exhibits and animal holding areas.  The Dallas Zoo Storm Water Wetland SEP shall include collection infrastructure; a separator or separators to reduce the presence of floatable materials and reduce sediment load in the runoff; small biological-treatment facilities (also called  package treatment plants ), a wetland, and a means of returning water (after final treatment in the wetland) to the  Zoo for use in irrigation.  The SEP shall be designed and constructed so that it can accept runoff from at least 15 acres of the Zoo's Wilds of Africa Exhibit, and a greater number of acres if possible.  The SEP shall be designed and constructed to maximize the amount of treated water that can be diverted back to the Zoo for use in drip irrigation and minimize the amount of water discharged to Cedar Creek.  The wetland component of the SEP shall be located adjacent to or near Cedar Creek, on the west side of E. Clarendon Drive.  The wetland shall slowly filter and biologically treat storm water and any wash water entering the wetland, both to prepare the water for use in drip irrigation and to reduce the pollutant load in discharges of water from the Zoo to Cedar Creek.  The primary objective of this SEP is to improve the quality and reduce the impact of discharges from the Zoo's storm water system to Cedar Creek.

Water quality samples shall be taken over a three-year period on a frequent basis, such as quarterly, and after a significant rainfall event at a minimum of five sampling locations along the Delaware River in Texas and New Mexico. Samples shall be tested for physical and chemical parameters associated with aquatic life and shall be tested by an independent, accredited laboratory. The data collected from this SEP shall be made available to the public on the internet and Respondent shall provide notice to the EPA, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Bureau of Land Management, Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, Texas Parks and Wildlife Department, New Mexico Environment Department, and New Mexico Department of Game and Fish when data collected from this SEP is made available on the internet within five (5) days of when such data is placed on the internet.

CARGILL HAS HISTORICALLY STORED GASEOUS SULFUR DIOXIDE AT CORN WET MILLING FACILITIES FOR USE IN THE PRODUCTION PROCESS.  GASEOUS SULFUR DIOXIDE IS VIEWED AS POSING SIGNIFICANT ENVIRONMENTAL AND HEALTH RISKS AND ITS STORAGE AND USE IS REGULATED UNDER 40 CRF PART 68 ( CHEMICAL ACCIDENT PREVENTION PROVISIONS) AND UNDER CFR PART 1910.119 (PROCESS SAFETY MANAGEMENT OF HIGHLY HAZARDOUS CHEMICALS).  GASEOUS SULFUR DIOXIDE STORAGE EXCEEDS THE 40 CFR PART 68 THRESHOLDS AT BLAIR, CEDAR, DAYTON, EDDYVILLE, AND MEMPHIS AND TOTAL GASEOUS SULFUR DIOXIDE STORAGE EXCEEDS 1.2 MILLION POUNDS AT THESE FACILITIES.  THIS PROJECT INVOLVES PERMANENT REPLACEMENT OF GASEOUS SULFUR DIOXIDE USED IN THE CORN WET MILLING PROCESS WITH A LESS HAZARDOUS SUBSTITUTE, LIQUID SODIUM BIOSULFIDE (SBS), WHICH IS NOT SUBJECT TO EITHER RISK MANAGEMENT OR PROCESS SAFETY PLAN REQUIREMENTS.  PROJECT SCOPE WILL INCLUDE INSTALLATION OF TANKS, PIPING, AND CONTROLS FOR SYSTEMS LOCATED IN BLAIR, CEDAR, DAYTON, EDDYVILLE, AND MEMPHIS, PURCHASE OF SBS, AND REMOVAL OF GASEOUS SO2 HANDLING CAPABILITIES.  THIS PROJECT WILL BENEFIT THE ENVIRONMENT BY ELIMINATING THE RISK OF SO2 RELEASES THROUGH THE REMOVAL OF OVER 1.2 MILLION POUNDS OF SULFUR DIOXIDE STORAGE AND REDUCED SO2 EMISSIONS FROM FACILITY PROCESSES.  IT IS ALSO ANTICIPATED THAT THIS PROJECT WOULD REDUCE FUGITIVE SULFUR DIOXIDE EMISSIONS.

Respondent will install and operate new ammonia leak detectors in the Low-Pressure Receiver room and in cold storage areas of the Facility, including near the following evaporators: Spiral Freezer #1, Spiral Freezer #2, Production Cooler #1, Production Cooler #2, Freezer #1, Back Freezer, and Shipping Cooler.  The new detectors are integrated into the ALCS to provide continuous monitoring information that will be used to automatically respond in the event of an ammonia release.  Respondent will install new solenoid valves to allow the ALCS to automatically operate in the event of a release.

Ammonia detectors will continuously monitor ammonia levels in the areas of the Facility listed above and will function as follows.  If a detector senses that ammonia concentration in its area rises to 25 parts per million (ppm), an alarm is activated to notify facility operators and ventilation is activated.  If ammonia concentration in the area continues to rise to 35 ppm, the ALCS automatically closes valves to halt the flow of ammonia (in both liquid and gaseous forms) to all evaporators in that area.  Compressors automatically begin operating to pull ammonia from the evaporators into a high-pressure receiver for storage.

Respondent will install and operate a Detection Status Screen which will provide real-time readings from every ammonia leak detector in the Facility.  It will be in a weathertight cabinet outside the main machinery room, allowing operators and emergency responders to view and monitor airborne levels of ammonia throughout the Facility prior to entry into a leak area.
